cards.front: In predator-prey dynamics, why is each population's per capita growth rate set by the other population's numbers?
cards.back: Every kill is entered twice: a death for the prey, and food that predators, on average, turn into births. So prey grow at r - aP each and predators at eaN - m each.
cards.quote: Every kill is entered in two ledgers: a death in the prey's, and food that, on average, the predators turn into births.

cards.front: How can a predator affect species it rarely or never eats, and even help some species it also eats?
cards.back: By changing the numbers or behaviour of the species in between. The size and even the sign of these effects depend on the community.
cards.quote: by changing the numbers or behaviour of the species in between.

cards.front: A {{c1::predator}} is a consumer that kills and eats other organisms, its prey.
cards.quote: A predator is a consumer that kills and eats other organisms, its prey.
cards.section: Two ledgers, written as equations

cards.front: Write the two equations of the classical Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model, with N prey and P predators.
cards.back: dN/dt = rN - aNP; dP/dt = eaNP - mP.
cards.quote: With N prey and P predators: dN/dt = rN - aNP dP/dt = eaNP - mP
cards.section: Two ledgers, written as equations

cards.front: In the Lotka-Volterra model, what is the attack rate a, and what are its units?
cards.back: The risk of being caught that one predator adds to each prey, in per predator per day. So aP is each prey's death rate from predation, and aNP is prey eaten per day.
cards.quote: The attack rate a is the risk of being caught that one predator adds to each prey (units: per predator per day)
cards.section: Two ledgers, written as equations

cards.front: In the Lotka-Volterra model, what do the parameters e and m stand for?
cards.back: e: the average number of new predators made per prey eaten. m: the predators' per capita death rate (per day).
cards.quote: The conversion e is the average number of new predators made per prey eaten, and m is the predators' per capita death rate (per day).
cards.section: Two ledgers, written as equations

cards.front: List the main assumptions of the classical Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model.
cards.back: Without predators, prey grow exponentially (no carrying capacity); without prey, predators decline exponentially; intake rises in proportion to prey numbers with no handling time; well mixed, no age structure, no space, constant parameters.
cards.quote: Without predators the prey grow exponentially, with no carrying capacity.
cards.section: Two ledgers, written as equations

cards.front: Why does a predator in the classical Lotka-Volterra model never get full?
cards.back: Its intake rises in proportion to prey numbers, and the model has no handling time (time spent catching and eating each prey) to cap it.
cards.quote: Each predator's intake rises in proportion to prey numbers with no handling time
cards.section: Two ledgers, written as equations

cards.front: What is an isocline in the Lotka-Volterra model, and how do you find the prey and predator isoclines?
cards.back: The set of numbers at which one population stops changing. Set each per capita rate to zero: r - aP = 0 gives P = r/a; eaN - m = 0 gives N = m/(ea).
cards.quote: Set each per capita rate to zero: r - aP = 0 gives P = r/a, and eaN - m = 0 gives N = m/(ea).
cards.section: Two ledgers, written as equations

cards.front: In the classical Lotka-Volterra model, the equilibrium prey number is N* = {{c1::m/(ea)}}, and the predator number is P* = r/a.
cards.back: The equilibrium is where the two isoclines cross.
cards.quote: Where the two lines cross is the equilibrium: N = m/(ea) P = r/a
cards.section: Two ledgers, written as equations

cards.front: In the classical Lotka-Volterra model, the prey start breeding twice as fast (r doubles) and nothing else changes. At the new equilibrium, which is larger than before: the prey, the predators, or both?
cards.back: Only the predators. N* = m/(ea) contains no r, so prey equilibrium stays put; P* = r/a doubles.
cards.why: Each equilibrium is set by the other population's parameters: faster prey breeding feeds more predators, which eat the extra prey.
cards.quote: Each equilibrium is set by the other population's parameters: faster prey breeding feeds more predators, and the extra predators eat the extra prey.
cards.section: Two ledgers, written as equations

cards.front: Lotka-Volterra model with r = 1 per day, a = 0.01 per predator per day, e = 0.1 predators per prey eaten, m = 0.5 per day. With N = 400 prey and P = 50 predators, find dN/dt and dP/dt.
cards.back: Prey: rN = 400 born, aNP = 0.01 x 400 x 50 = 200 eaten, so dN/dt = +200 prey per day. Predators: eaNP = 0.1 x 200 = 20 made, mP = 25 die, so dP/dt = -5 predators per day.
cards.quote: Prey eaten are aNP = 0.01 x 400 x 50 = 200 prey per day.
cards.section: Two ledgers, written as equations

cards.front: Lotka-Volterra model with r = 1 per day, a = 0.01 per predator per day, e = 0.1 predators per prey eaten, m = 0.5 per day. Find the equilibrium numbers.
cards.section: Two ledgers, written as equations

cards.front: A Lotka-Volterra system has equilibrium N* = 500 prey and P* = 100 predators. It now holds 400 prey and 50 predators. Which population is rising and which is falling?
cards.back: Prey rise and predators fall (the bottom-left zone).
cards.why: Prey grow whenever P is below r/a; predators decline whenever N is below m/(ea).
cards.quote: Prey are below 500 and predators below 100: the bottom-left zone, where prey rise and predators fall.
cards.section: Two ledgers, written as equations

cards.front: What does it mean that the cycles of the classical Lotka-Volterra model are neutrally stable?
cards.back: There is a family of nested loops. A nudge moves the system onto another loop, and nothing pulls it back to one cycle, so the starting numbers set the amplitude.
cards.quote: a nudge moves it to another track, and it circles that one instead, with no single cycle pulling it back.
cards.section: What the classical cycle leaves out

cards.front: In the classical Lotka-Volterra model, why do the average numbers over any full loop equal the equilibrium numbers?
cards.back: Over one loop each population ends where it began, so its per capita rate averages zero. That requires the average of P to be r/a and of N to be m/(ea).
cards.quote: Over one loop each population ends where it began, so its per capita rate averages zero
cards.section: What the classical cycle leaves out

cards.front: Lotka-Volterra model with r = 1 per day, a = 0.01, e = 0.1, m = 0.5 per day. Both populations are harvested at the same per capita rate h = 0.1 per day. What are the average prey and predator numbers?
cards.back: Prey: (m + h)/(ea) = 0.6/0.001 = 600. Predators: (r - h)/a = 0.9/0.01 = 90. Prey up from 500, predators down from 100.
cards.quote: harvest both populations at the same per capita rate h, and the averages become (m + h)/(ea) prey and (r - h)/a predators
cards.section: What the classical cycle leaves out

cards.front: A crop pest and its insect predator follow the classical Lotka-Volterra model. An insecticide kills both at the same per capita rate, below the pest's r. In the model, what happens to the average pest and predator numbers?
cards.back: The pest average rises to (m + h)/(ea) and the predator average falls to (r - h)/a.
cards.why: Rests on Volterra's harvest rule: equal per capita harvest moves prey up and predators down, as long as h stays below r.
cards.quote: prey up and predators down, as long as h stays below r so that predators persist.
cards.section: What the classical cycle leaves out

cards.front: Lotka-Volterra prey (r = 1, a = 0.01, e = 0.1, m = 0.5 per day) are given a carrying capacity K = 400, so without predators they settle at 400. Can the predators persist?
cards.back: No. Predators replace themselves only when prey exceed N* = 500. At 400 prey a rare predator's rate is 0.001 x 400 - 0.5 = -0.1 per day, so predators die out and prey settle at 400.
cards.quote: Each predator replaces itself only when prey exceed N* = 500.
cards.section: What the classical cycle leaves out

cards.front: What does prey self-limitation (logistic growth with carrying capacity K) do to Lotka-Volterra cycles?
cards.back: The neutral cycles disappear. If K is above N*, the populations settle at equilibrium, often through damped oscillations, and P* falls below r/a. If K is below N*, predators die out.
cards.quote: If K is above N, the populations settle at the equilibrium, often through damped oscillations
cards.section: What the classical cycle leaves out

cards.front: Lotka-Volterra model with r = 1, a = 0.01, e = 0.1, m = 0.5 per day, now with logistic prey and K = 1000. The prey isocline tilts to P = (r/a)(1 - N/K). What is the equilibrium?
cards.back: N* stays m/(ea) = 500 prey. P* = 100 x (1 - 500/1000) = 50 predators, below r/a = 100.
cards.quote: the prey line tilts to P = (r/a)(1 - N/K), so the predator equilibrium falls below r/a
cards.section: What the classical cycle leaves out

cards.front: What can adding handling time (so predators get full) do to a Lotka-Volterra model with logistic prey?
cards.back: For some parameters the model settles onto one limit cycle whose size does not depend on the start; for others it settles at an equilibrium, or the predators die out.
cards.quote: Handling time as well, so predators get full
cards.section: What the classical cycle leaves out

cards.front: A predator-prey model is knocked off its cycle and returns to a cycle of the same size. Is this the classical Lotka-Volterra model or a version with handling time and logistic prey? Why?
cards.back: The version with handling time: for some parameter values it has a limit cycle whose size does not depend on the start. Classical neutral loops would keep the new, different orbit.
cards.quote: For some parameter values the model settles onto one cycle whose size does not depend on the start
cards.section: What the classical cycle leaves out

cards.front: In classical Lotka-Volterra cycles, why does the predator peak come after the prey peak?
cards.back: Prey peak when rising predators pass r/a. Predators keep rising while prey stay above m/(ea), so they peak later, when the falling prey drop below m/(ea).
cards.why: Rests on the rule that each population's per capita rate is set by the other's numbers.
cards.quote: So each population's per capita (per individual) growth rate is set by the other's numbers

cards.front: Near equilibrium, a Lotka-Volterra cycle takes about 2 pi / square root of (rm). Find the period for r = 2 per day and m = 0.5 per day.
cards.back: square root of (2 x 0.5) = 1, so the period is about 6.28 days. This is a small-amplitude approximation; the larger orbit through (400, 50) takes about 9.3 days.
cards.quote: Near the equilibrium the cycle takes about 2 pi / square root of (rm)
cards.section: The period of the cycle

cards.front: Paine removed the sea star Pisaster from a patch of rocky shore at Mukkaw Bay. What happened to the number of species holding space on the rock?
cards.back: It fell from 15 to 8 in the removal patch; the adjacent control did not lose species in the same way.
cards.quote: The film's count of 15 to 8 covered only species holding space on the rock
cards.section: What one shore can and cannot show

cards.front: What is a keystone species?
cards.back: A species whose effect on the community is large relative to its abundance. The most common species is not a keystone by default.
cards.quote: The keystone label compares effect with abundance, so the most common species is not a keystone by default
cards.section: What one shore can and cannot show

cards.front: At Mukkaw Bay, mussels covered the rock once Pisaster was gone. Why was Pisaster, not the mussels, the keystone?
cards.back: Mussels were the dominant competitor, winning the contest for space. Pisaster had the effect out of proportion to its abundance: by eating mussels it kept space open for other species.
cards.quote: at Mukkaw Bay the mussels were the dominant competitor (the winner of the contest for space), and Pisaster was the keystone.
cards.section: What one shore can and cannot show

cards.front: What makes up a predator's net effect on another species in a community?
cards.back: Its direct effects (killing it, or changing how it behaves) plus effects passed through other species. The two can pull in opposite directions.
cards.quote: A predator's net effect on a species combines its direct effects (killing it, or changing how it behaves) with effects passed through other species
cards.section: What one shore can and cannot show

cards.front: On a rocky shore, Pisaster has a direct cost for chitons and also eats the mussels that compete with them for space. Predict what happens to chitons in a patch after Pisaster is removed.
cards.back: Chitons (and larger limpets) leave the patch for lack of space and food: there the indirect help outweighed the direct cost.
cards.quote: Larger limpets left the patch as well as the chitons, so there the indirect help won
cards.section: What one shore can and cannot show

cards.front: Does a keystone predator always raise species richness?
cards.back: No. A weaker species gains only if release from the dominant competitor outweighs what the predator costs it directly; heavier predation can reverse that balance.
cards.quote: A weaker species gains only if release from the dominant competitor outweighs what the predator costs it directly
cards.section: What one shore can and cannot show

cards.front: Removing Pisaster lowered the number of species holding space on the rock. If species living among the mussels were also counted, could the conclusion change?
cards.back: Yes. A mussel bed is itself a habitat, sheltering over 300 associated species, so community-wide richness could rise. The answer depends on which species are counted.
cards.quote: A mussel bed is itself a habitat: count the species living among the mussels and the result can reverse
cards.section: What one shore can and cannot show

cards.front: A {{c1::trophic level}} is a feeding position in a food chain: plants, herbivores, carnivores.
cards.quote: A trophic level is a feeding position in a food chain: plants, herbivores, carnivores.
cards.section: Cascades through killing and through fear

cards.front: A {{c1::trophic cascade}} is an indirect predator effect that extends through several trophic levels: predator to herbivore to plant.
cards.quote: A trophic cascade is an indirect predator effect that extends through several trophic levels: predator to herbivore to plant.
cards.section: Cascades through killing and through fear

cards.front: An Aleutian island with many sea otters had few urchins and dense kelp; an island without otters had many urchins and little kelp. Why does this fit a cascade but not prove one?
cards.back: Otters eat urchins and urchins graze kelp, so the pattern is what a two-link cascade predicts. But it is a comparison between places and no one removed otters, so other island differences could contribute.
cards.quote: Otters eat urchins, and urchins graze kelp, so the urchin and kelp pattern fits a two-link cascade, but no one removed otters.
cards.section: Cascades through killing and through fear

cards.front: When sea otters declined across western Alaska in the 1990s, what happened to urchins and kelp?
cards.back: Urchins increased and kelp beds were lost. The otter decline was probably because killer whales ate more of them.
cards.quote: when sea otters declined across western Alaska in the 1990s, probably because killer whales ate more of them, urchins increased and kelp beds were lost.
cards.section: Cascades through killing and through fear

cards.front: Distinguish a density-mediated from a trait-mediated trophic cascade.
cards.back: Density-mediated: predators kill herbivores, so fewer are left to eat plants. Trait-mediated: predation risk (fear) changes what surviving herbivores do.
cards.quote: A trait-mediated cascade works by changing what surviving herbivores do, through the risk of being eaten: fear.
cards.section: Cascades through killing and through fear

cards.front: In old-field enclosures, grasshoppers were kept with no spiders, with hunting spiders, or with spiders whose mouthparts were glued so they could not kill. What did the glued-spider treatment test, and what did it show?
cards.back: It separated fear from killing. Plants with glued spiders looked like those with hunting spiders, because grasshoppers changed how long they fed and what they ate; the plant effect was traced to risk, not deaths.
cards.quote: The authors traced the plant effect to risk rather than deaths, and not every plant benefited.
cards.section: Cascades through killing and through fear

cards.front: Suppose a spider's effect on plants worked only by killing grasshoppers. In an enclosure test with spiders that cannot kill, what would the plants look like?
cards.back: Like plants with no spiders: spiders that cannot kill remove no grasshoppers.
cards.why: A density-mediated cascade needs deaths. The observed match with hunting spiders is what pointed to fear.
cards.quote: A density-mediated cascade works by killing herbivores, so fewer are left to eat plants.
cards.section: Cascades through killing and through fear

cards.front: Why is the claim that reintroduced wolves caused willow recovery in Yellowstone still open?
cards.back: Wolves were never an experimental treatment. In a ten-year experiment, reducing browsing alone did not bring willows to the 2-metre recovery height, and how to measure recovery is disputed.
cards.quote: reducing browsing alone did not bring the willows to the 2-metre height they used as their recovery criterion
cards.section: Cascades through killing and through fear

cards.front: A 2025 review counted predator-manipulation tests of keystone predation. What did it find, and why is it not an estimate of how common keystone predation is?
cards.back: Of 25 publications, 10 reported consistent support, 7 context dependence and 8 none. The search relied on the term itself, and a vote count is not a frequency estimate.
cards.why: So a keystone result on one shore is a hypothesis for the next shore.
cards.quote: 10 reported consistent support, 7 found the effect context-dependent and 8 found none
cards.section: How far one system generalizes

cards.front: Design a study testing whether keystone predation by Pisaster generalizes across a coast. What would you replicate, measure, and count as evidence against generality?
cards.back: Many sites differing in wave exposure and mussel recruitment; random removal and control plots at each; survey before and yearly after (before-after-control-impact); a fixed taxa list; mussel cover. Richness falling where recruitment is high and changing little where it is low means real but conditional.
cards.quote: Survey every plot before removal and yearly for several years after (a before-after-control-impact design), to separate a change from what was already happening.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In a Pisaster removal study, why measure mussel cover in every plot, not just species richness?
cards.back: It tests the mechanism: if removal lowers richness through mussel takeover, mussel cover should rise first.
cards.quote: if removal lowers richness, mussel cover should rise first, which tests the mechanism.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Why is the sea-star wasting die-off from 2013 a weaker test of keystone predation than a removal experiment?
cards.back: It is a natural experiment: shores that lost most of their Pisaster can be compared with shores that lost fewer, but the die-off was not randomly assigned, so the shores may differ in other ways.
cards.quote: the die-off was not randomly assigned.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Why is the famous hare and lynx cycle weak evidence for Lotka-Volterra cycles?
cards.back: It comes from fur-trade records, which reflect trapping effort as well as animal numbers.
cards.quote: The famous hare and lynx cycle comes from fur-trade records, which reflect trapping effort as well as animal numbers.
cards.section: Real data rarely fit the classical model

cards.front: Predatory and plant-eating mites coexisted on oranges only when the arena was made patchy. Which assumption of the classical Lotka-Volterra model does this challenge?
cards.back: That populations are well mixed, with no space. Coexistence depended on spatial structure the model leaves out.
cards.quote: Carl Huffaker could keep predatory and plant-eating mites coexisting on oranges only when he made the arena patchy
cards.section: Real data rarely fit the classical model
